title: Putting target selection to the test
lead: In ManipScope, a virtual test from the University of Science and Technology of China and its partners, the arrangement of objects stays fixed. The team changes the instruction to see whether the robot controller selects the newly named target.

news.title: One scene, several commands: testing target selection
news.summary: A team led by researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China introduced ManipScope, a simulated test for robot controllers. It holds the arrangement of objects fixed and checks whether the controller chooses a new target when the instruction changes.
news.details: The test suite contains 48 held-out simulation scenes. In ten target-selection scenes, the team changed instructions while keeping the starting arrangement fixed.
news.technical_novelty: ManipScope tests whether a robot controller changes its action when the instruction names a different object or destination.
news.engineering_impact: The results help isolate errors in selecting a target before assessing execution of the chosen movement.
news.limitations: The study ran in simulation and withheld demonstrations for the held-out scenes.
news.evidence_status: The researchers reported their results and control runs in a preprint.
news.organization: University of Science and Technology of China, Sharpa Robotics, Shanghai Jiao Tong University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
news.body:
Researchers from the University of Science and Technology of China, Sharpa Robotics and two other universities built ManipScope on resources from the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator. Their test scores robot controllers that must select an object or destination from a written command. It measures whether each controller can execute every instruction presented for a starting state, with the state reset between trials.

The team organized the tasks into six families and withheld demonstrations for the 48 evaluation scenes. To test the role of the instruction, it reused starting arrangements and varied the command in ten target-selection scenes. A single successful attempt can happen if a model picks the object that tends to appear in a familiar location. A series of instructions tests whether the same model can take the correct action for each command from an identical starting state.

Pooling the results of ten saved model versions, the team reported that all instructions were followed in 39 of 1,000 states, or 3.9%. A control that received no instruction text scored 16% on that measure. In a separate analysis of 12 model versions across 13,200 runs in 11 scenes, 84.6% of failed attempts involved moving a distractor, an object that was present but was not the intended target. The two figures count different things: one counts complete sets of instructions and the other describes how individual attempts failed.

Reusing an initial state holds scene geometry fixed while the instruction changes, so the two factors can be studied separately. A separate positive control used a general-purpose model with a different interface to the simulator and solved 44 of 50 states, or 88%. This helps establish that the target tasks can be solved under the test conditions. The interface difference matters when interpreting the gap, and the experiment gives no corresponding score for robots facing camera noise or changes in physical contact.

news.title: A six-camera headset records hand movements for robot learning
news.summary: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot described RoboCap-10k, a dataset of people doing physical work. The headset combines several viewpoints and motion readings so the researchers can estimate head and hand movement in three dimensions.
news.details: Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot collected 10,000 hours of recordings of human work in 11 countries.
news.technical_novelty: A headset with six synchronized cameras and inertial sensors supports three-dimensional estimates of head and hand movement.
news.engineering_impact: The recordings provide examples of physical tasks for teams developing robot learning systems.
news.limitations: The data contain no force or touch measurements. The paper does not evaluate training on a robot.
news.evidence_status: The authors describe the dataset, hardware and processing in a preprint.
news.body:
Grounded Superintelligence and BitRobot presented RoboCap-10k, a collection of first-person recordings of people handling objects at work. Its purpose is to retain the geometry of those movements in a form that can be used to develop robot controllers. The preprint describes how the team records synchronized images and reconstructs the positions of the wearer’s head and hands.

The 250-gram headset carries six synchronized cameras and two inertial measurement units that measure acceleration and rotation. The cameras view the wearer's hands from different angles. The processing combines the views and sensor readings to estimate head motion and three-dimensional hand positions. Each recording session has its own calibration, which lets the processing account for the positions and characteristics of the cameras.

The authors selected 10,000 hours of elapsed recording time. A minute filmed by several cameras counts as one minute. They segmented recordings from 11 countries into 1,378,462 clips with a median duration of 17.8 seconds. The authors say participants gave written consent and were compensated for taking part. Audio is excluded and faces are obscured.

The headset's path is estimated from images and inertial data. To reconstruct the hands, the processing fits MANO, a model of the shape and joints of a human hand, to the observations. The resulting trajectories are estimates derived from the recordings. They give developers a geometric description of the movement, but no direct measurement of contact or force. The paper does not measure what a robot can do after training on this collection.

news.title: OMRON specifies new mobile carriers for metre-wide aisles
news.summary: OMRON Robotics opened orders in the Americas and Europe for the LD-150 and LD-300 indoor carriers. The company published their dimensions, speed and fleet coordination features for sites with narrow aisles.
news.details: OMRON Robotics opened orders for two indoor carriers rated for 150 and 300 kilograms.
news.technical_novelty: The carriers navigate using their surroundings without floor markers, while fleet software assigns transport jobs.
news.engineering_impact: A site trial can establish how room to manoeuvre, charging and traffic in both directions affect the amount moved per shift.
news.limitations: The published figures are product specifications. The company expects shipments to start in January 2027.
news.evidence_status: The source is the manufacturer, whose announcement gives no throughput measurements from a customer site.
news.body:
OMRON Robotics began taking orders in the Americas and Europe for two autonomous mobile robots, the LD-150 and LD-300. These vehicles carry loads inside buildings, estimate their position from the surroundings and follow assigned routes. The specifications give vehicle widths and supported operating limits for buyers evaluating a retrofit where existing aisles cannot easily be widened.

The smaller LD-150 is rated to carry 150 kg and is 500 mm wide. For the LD-300 the corresponding figures are 300 kg and 580 mm. OMRON specifies operation in aisles as narrow as one metre, a series top speed of 2.1 m/s and the ability to handle a slope of up to five degrees. The vehicles estimate their position using features in their surroundings and do not require guide tape or floor markers.

OMRON's FLOW Core software assigns jobs, plans routes and coordinates the movements of the fleet. The vendor says it can manage up to 100 compatible OMRON vehicles of different types. Inductive charging transfers power at a station without a plug and can take as little as 18 minutes according to the company. Orders opened in the Americas and Europe, with other regions to follow. The vendor expects shipments to begin in January 2027.

For a turning envelope, engineers need both the carrier dimensions and the space occupied by the load as it swings around a corner. The announcement states an aisle width for travel and gives separate limits for payload, speed and grade. It gives no operating envelope for those limits in combination or traffic measurements for intersecting routes. A steep approach that leads directly into a turn would require more evidence than those headline specifications provide.

news.title: Outsight runs 3D tracking on a Xeon-based local server
news.summary: Outsight announced that Shift, its moving-object tracker, runs on Microsoft's Azure Local platform. The configuration uses an Intel Xeon 6 central processor with matrix acceleration to process sensor readings.
news.details: Outsight announced that its three-dimensional tracking software runs on Intel-based servers managed through Azure Local.
news.technical_novelty: The system processes sensor readings, including laser scans, into an updating representation of moving objects.
news.engineering_impact: The described configuration runs on a central processor and gives customers a way to process the data on site.
news.limitations: Outsight claims a delay under 50 milliseconds without the measurement conditions needed for comparison. It provides no accuracy or cost figures.
news.evidence_status: Outsight reported the integration and did not include an independent test.
news.body:
Outsight announced an integration for Shift, software that tracks object positions from streams of sensor measurements. It runs on customer-site servers administered through Azure Local, Microsoft's system for managing local computing infrastructure. The announcement identifies the compute hardware and where the workload runs, giving engineers a specific configuration to examine.

Outsight highlights lidar, a sensor that measures distances with pulses of laser light. The software uses those measurements to update the positions of objects moving through three-dimensional space. According to the company, the laser data can be combined with readings from other systems, including cameras or Wi-Fi. Outsight describes the output as anonymized and includes no independent audit of that claim.

The described setup uses an Intel Xeon 6 system-on-chip, a processor package that integrates key computing and support functions. It uses Intel AMX, on-chip hardware for speeding up matrix operations. In this configuration the tracking workload runs on the central processor without a separate graphics accelerator. Outsight claims a processing delay below 50 milliseconds without giving the conditions for that figure. The company announced a planned demonstration at Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco, which ran from November 17 to 20.

A comparison between compute platforms would require a fixed load: the same number of sensors, the same input rate and the same number of objects under tracking. With that held steady, the time from sensor input to a position update could show the effect of changing the hardware. The release supplies no measurements under such conditions. It describes a supported configuration and leaves the latency and throughput limits for that configuration open.

news.title: Huang returns to NVIDIA while export oversight stays with a board committee
news.summary: NVIDIA announced on November 23 that Jensen Huang was back as chief executive and a director. A separate committee continues to oversee exports at the robotics computing supplier, and the internal inquiry remains open.
news.details: The board reinstated Huang as president, chief executive and director. Colette Kress remains chief financial officer.
news.technical_novelty: A planned compliance chief complements the board’s national security and export control committee.
news.engineering_impact: A computing supplier used by robotics teams is changing how it oversees trade compliance.
news.limitations: The independent internal inquiry continues. The announcement gives no revised hardware delivery terms.
news.evidence_status: NVIDIA’s announcement, its filing with the US securities regulator and Reuters confirm the leadership decision.
news.body:
NVIDIA’s board returned Jensen Huang to the positions of president and chief executive and restored his seat as a director. NVIDIA announced the decision on November 23. For engineering teams, this changes the leadership of a supplier whose processors can be used both to train robot control models and to run them once they have been trained.

In its filing with the US securities regulator, NVIDIA dates the board action to November 22. The company made it public the following day, and Reuters independently reported Huang’s return. The directors voted unanimously. Colette Kress, who had been running the company on an interim basis, remains chief financial officer. Harvey Jones stays on as board chair.

The board said it had heard from senior US government officials and believes Huang’s return poses no national security risk. That is the board’s assessment. NVIDIA says it created a committee of independent directors after reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The committee and its outside counsel will continue the inquiry. NVIDIA also began looking for a company-wide compliance chief to oversee adherence to rules. Its board has a dedicated committee supervising national security and export control.

An engineering group choosing computing resources for more than one site faces two separate questions. The first is whether a processor can handle work such as images from several cameras within the time available. The second is whether a specific unit can be supplied to the intended recipient. This announcement describes NVIDIA’s leadership and who oversees compliance. It gives no revised terms for particular processors, countries or end users. An engineer who has qualified hardware for a workload still needs transaction-specific information before planning a delivery.

technology_signal.title: Scoring controllers across a set of commands
technology_signal.summary: The University of Science and Technology of China and its partners measure whether a controller can follow every instruction given the same starting layout. They report results for complete command sets and separately analyze failed attempts.
technology_signal.implications: Repeating the test requires resetting the scene and specifying a different correct target for each relevant command. The published measurements come from simulation.
